title: Tools as altar vessels (Rule 31)
hookLine: the cellarer treats pots and tools like the vessels of the altar

lines: AS IF THEY WERE ALTAR VESSELS.
cards: A dented saucepan. A spade with a split handle. A ladle left in the sink.
Nobody would put them in a church. Yesterday the cooks handed the pots back to someone. Meet him.
He's called the cellarer: the monk who keeps the stores, the food, the tools, the household goods. Benedict gives him a whole chapter, and in it one instruction turns the storeroom upside down.
He is to look on every vessel and every possession of the monastery as if they were the sacred vessels of the altar. The chalice and the saucepan, handled with the same care.

teach.h: A STEADY MAN FOR THE STORES.
teach.b: Start with the man Benedict wants for the job: wise, steady, sober, not a big eater, not proud, not touchy, not slow, not wasteful, not stingy. Someone who'll be, the Rule says, like a father to the whole community.
He looks after the sick, the children, guests and the poor. He lets nothing be neglected. And he treats the hoe and the bowl as if they belonged on the altar.
Why would a pot be holy? One way to read it: in Benedict's house, there's no clean line where the sacred stops and the ordinary starts.

teach.h: NO LINE BETWEEN ALTAR AND STOVE.
teach.b: The same God honored at the altar in the morning is served at the stove at noon. Carelessness with things is, in its small way, carelessness with the people who need them and the God who gave them.
An old prophecy in Zechariah pictures this. On that day, even the bells on the horses carry the words holiness unto the Lord, and the temple pots are like the bowls before the altar.
Then: "every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be holiness unto the LORD of hosts." Every pot. The same chapter carries this care over to people.

If a brother asks for something unreasonable, the cellarer mustn't sadden him with scorn. He should refuse humbly, and give a reason. And if he has nothing to give, he should at least give a kind word.

teach.h: A GOOD WORD ABOVE THE BEST GIFT.
teach.b: A good word, the Rule says, borrowing from the book of Sirach, is above the best gift. A pot handled gently. A brother answered gently.
The same care, pointed two ways.

how: In Benedictine houses the cellarer, or a monk or nun in that role, keeps the community's stores and goods, and the Rule's call to treat ordinary things as altar vessels shapes how the house's tools, kitchens and workshops are kept.

games.q: what does “tools as altar vessels” mean?
o: melting old tools down to make church bells
treating every pot and tool as sacred
using kitchen tools in the church service

games.q: the cellarer's care — tap the pairs.
p: like a sacred vessel of the altar
every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah

s: the cellarer's chapter is only about food and tools
it's about people too: refuse humbly, and give a good word when you've nothing to give.
Benedict asks him to treat pots like the vessels of the altar
every vessel and possession of the monastery, as if sacred vessels of the altar.
Benedict wants a strict, stingy man for the stores
not wasteful, not stingy: like a father to the whole community.

games.q: you're the cellarer. a brother asks for something the house can't spare, and he's being unreasonable about it. what does the Rule ask?
o: tell him plainly how silly the request is.
refuse humbly, give a reason, and a good word.
give it to him to keep the peace.
games.why: the cellarer mustn't sadden the brother with contempt: refuse humbly, with reason, and if there's nothing to give, give a good word.

practice: Pick up a tool that's near you, a mug, a pen, a knife, your phone, or picture one you use every day.

Notice its weight, its scratches, the places your hand has worn, who made it and who it has fed or helped; later, clean it slowly, the way you'd handle something precious. If you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Tools as altar vessels. Benedict's word to his cellarer: treat every pot and tool as a sacred vessel of the altar.

orig.note: Latin, from Rule chapter thirty-one: the consecrated vessels of the altar.

carryVoice: Your line: every pot is holy. The saucepan too, handled like the chalice. Same time tomorrow.
